items.stem: “Herzberg’s two-factor theory of job satisfaction has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including research base in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It led to job enrichment programmes that give employees more responsibility and recognition. Strength (research base): It was based on detailed accounts of real experiences at work using the critical incident technique. Weakness (generalisability): The original sample was about 200 engineers and accountants, so it may not apply to manual or low-paid workers. Weakness (self-serving bias): People tend to credit themselves for good events and blame the context for bad events, which may explain the two factors. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: A student writes: “Herzberg argued that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are opposite ends of one scale.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. He argued they are separate dimensions caused by different factors.

items.stem: Explain the difference between hygiene factors and motivators.
items.answer: Hygiene factors (pay, conditions, supervision, policy) are about the job context: when poor they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them only removes dissatisfaction. Motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, the work itself, advancement) are about job content and produce satisfaction and motivation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hygiene; 1 mark motivators; 1 mark difference in effect [3]

items.stem: Lucas, an occupational psychologist in Kathmandu, used the Job Diagnostic Survey (scores 1–7) to rate two jobs. For a laboratory technician: skill variety 6, task identity 7, task significance 3, autonomy 4, feedback 3. For a graphic designer: skill variety 4, task identity 1, task significance 5, autonomy 3, feedback 1. Motivating potential score (MPS) = ((skill variety + task identity + task significance) ÷ 3) × autonomy × feedback. What is the MPS for a laboratory technician, to one decimal place?

Leila, an occupational psychologist in Kathmandu, used the Job Diagnostic Survey (scores 1–7) to rate two jobs. For a hospital porter: skill variety 4, task identity 3, task significance 4, autonomy 1, feedback 2. For a laboratory technician: skill variety 3, task identity 2, task significance 6, autonomy 2, feedback 4. Motivating potential score (MPS) = ((skill variety + task identity + task significance) ÷ 3) × autonomy × feedback. Calculate the MPS for a laboratory technician and state which job has the higher motivating potential.
items.answer: 29.3; a laboratory technician
items.markingKey: ((3 + 2 + 6) ÷ 3) × 2 × 4 = 29.3. 1 mark MPS; 1 mark comparison [2]

items.stem: Jonas, an occupational psychologist in Hanoi, used the Job Diagnostic Survey (scores 1–7) to rate two jobs. items.stem: Assess the view that questionnaires are the best way to measure job satisfaction. In your answer, you may refer to social desirability and reliability.
items.answer: Arguments for: Standardised scales such as the JDI and MSQ give quantitative, comparable data from many employees. They can measure different facets of satisfaction. Arguments against: Employees may give socially desirable answers if they fear managers will see them. Fixed questions miss the reasons for dissatisfaction, which interviews can reveal. Behavioural measures such as absence and turnover may be more objective. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Explain the three components of Meyer and Allen’s model of organisational commitment.
items.answer: Affective: wanting to stay because of emotional attachment; continuance: needing to stay because leaving is costly (pay, pension, few alternatives); normative: feeling obliged to stay because of loyalty or a sense of duty.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Meyer and Allen’s three-component model of organisational commitment. Include at least one point about cultural bias.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It helps organisations see that employees may stay for different reasons and target affective commitment, which predicts performance best. Strength (measurement): Each component can be measured with standardised questionnaire scales. Weakness (cultural bias): The model was developed in Western organisations and may work differently in collectivist cultures. Weakness (overlap): Affective and normative commitment are highly correlated, so they may not be separate components. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: A company in Singapore enriched the jobs of 7 assembly workers (giving them responsibility for a whole product and quality checks) and compared their satisfaction scores (out of 50) with 7 workers on the unchanged assembly line. items.stem: A company in Jakarta with 40 employees, each scheduled to work 230 days a year, recorded 500 days lost to absence last year. Employee C had 1 separate spell of absence totalling 6 days. Employee D had 7 separate spells of absence totalling 12 days. The Bradford factor = S² × D, where S is the number of spells and D the total days absent. (a) Calculate the lost-time rate (percentage of scheduled working days lost to absence). Give your answer to one decimal place. (b) Calculate the Bradford factor for employee C and for employee D.
“Meyer and Allen’s three-component model of organisational commitment has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including usefulness in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (measurement): Each component can be measured with standardised questionnaire scales. Strength (usefulness): It helps organisations see that employees may stay for different reasons and target affective commitment, which predicts performance best. Weakness (overlap): Affective and normative commitment are highly correlated, so they may not be separate components. Weakness (cultural bias): The model was developed in Western organisations and may work differently in collectivist cultures. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “In Herzberg’s theory, features of the job content such as achievement, recognition and responsibility that cause satisfaction”.
items.answer: Motivators
items.markingKey: Motivators: in Herzberg’s theory, features of the job content such as achievement, recognition and responsibility that cause satisfaction. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the difference between hygiene factors and motivators. (b) A student writes: “Herzberg argued that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are opposite ends of one scale.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Hygiene factors (pay, conditions, supervision, policy) are about the job context: when poor they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them only removes dissatisfaction. Motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, the work itself, advancement) are about job content and produce satisfaction and motivation. (b) Not correct. He argued they are separate dimensions caused by different factors.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark hygiene; 1 mark motivators; 1 mark difference in effect [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Felix, an occupational psychologist in Madrid, used the Job Diagnostic Survey (scores 1–7) to rate two jobs. For a bus driver: skill variety 3, task identity 5, task significance 7, autonomy 1, feedback 7. For a graphic designer: skill variety 4, task identity 6, task significance 3, autonomy 7, feedback 6. Motivating potential score (MPS) = ((skill variety + task identity + task significance) ÷ 3) × autonomy × feedback. Calculate the MPS for a graphic designer and state which job has the higher motivating potential.
items.answer: 182.0; a graphic designer
items.markingKey: ((4 + 6 + 3) ÷ 3) × 7 × 6 = 182.0. 1 mark MPS; 1 mark comparison [2]

items.stem: Isla compared job satisfaction scores (out of 50) for 7 employees whose jobs had been enriched and 7 whose jobs had not. items.answer: Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.

items.stem: Kwame collected job satisfaction scores and the number of days absent in the last year for 8 employees at a company in Muscat. items.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables are related; neither was manipulated, so the direction of cause is unknown and a third variable, such as health problems, could affect both.

items.stem: Design a field experiment to investigate whether job rotation increases satisfaction among supermarket staff. Your plan must include: ethical issues, controls and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: job rotation or fixed role; DV: job satisfaction score. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Cape Town, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “A single overall rating of job satisfaction tells managers exactly which aspect of the job needs improving.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Anonymous questionnaires are likely to give more valid answers about satisfaction.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Facet measures such as the JDI or MSQ are needed to identify the problem area. (b) Correct. Employees are less afraid of consequences, reducing social desirability.

items.stem: A hotel chain in Bogotá wants to find out why staff turnover is high. The manager plans to ask staff one question: “Are you happy at work? Yes/No.” (a) Explain two problems with this question. (b) Suggest a better way to measure job satisfaction and explain why. (c) Suggest how qualitative data could also be collected.
items.answer: (a) It gives no information about which aspects of work cause dissatisfaction, and a yes/no answer cannot show degrees of satisfaction. (b) Use an anonymous standardised facet questionnaire such as the JDI or short-form MSQ with rating scales, which shows the level of satisfaction with each aspect. (c) Exit interviews or an open question asking staff what they would change.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark method; 1 mark reason [2] (c) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which questionnaires are the best way to measure job satisfaction.
items.answer: Arguments for: Standardised scales such as the JDI and MSQ give quantitative, comparable data from many employees. They can measure different facets of satisfaction. Arguments against: Employees may give socially desirable answers if they fear managers will see them. Fixed questions miss the reasons for dissatisfaction, which interviews can reveal. Behavioural measures such as absence and turnover may be more objective. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.
